title: Rocket Report: SpaceX says no thanks to military launches; Spanish rocket nearly ready
gist: Rocket Report 9.16 says the US launch market is supply-constrained: SpaceX turned down three Space Force NSSL missions, no other provider bid, and SpaceX is declining new Falcon contracts generally. Blue Origin is scaling New Glenn to more than 100 Florida launches a year, and a NASA safety panel estimates about 22 Starship refuelings per lunar landing, which Musk says should be 6 to 8. Other items cover PLD Space, Reaction Dynamics, Ariane 6's return to flight, Japan's MMX launch and LandSpace debris found in Minnesota.

themes.theme: US national security launch capacity crunch

insights.claim: SpaceX declined to offer launch services for three future Space Force satellite missions listed through the National Security Space Launch program, two of them for the Space Development Agency, and no other rocket company offered to take them either, according to Politico.
insights.speaker: Eric Berger
insights.so_what: The US government has a shortage of launch supply, which gives pricing power to whoever has capacity and raises the strategic value of new medium- and heavy-lift entrants.
insights.locator: SpaceX says no thanks to Space

insights.claim: SpaceX has been declining to sign new Falcon 9 and Falcon Heavy launch contracts for all kinds of customers, while the alternative providers United Launch Alliance and Blue Origin are both working through setbacks with their vehicles.
insights.speaker: Eric Berger
insights.so_what: As SpaceX winds down new Falcon sales before Starship is ready, the market has a gap that rivals have not yet been able to fill.
insights.locator: SpaceX has been declining to sign

insights.claim: Brig. Gen. Eric Zarybnisky, the Space Force's acting portfolio acquisition executive, acknowledged growing pains as demand for rockets rises but expects Blue Origin and ULA to resolve their technical problems and new competitors to start flying in time.
insights.speaker: Eric Berger
insights.so_what: Watch whether Blue Origin and ULA hit their flight cadence; DoD payload schedules depend on it.
insights.quote: “Temporarily, there are some things we’ll need to work through, again, as we get new providers flying,”
insights.locator: A top Space Force official, Brig.

insights.claim: Blue Origin announced a major expansion of its Florida launch facilities with the goal of eventually flying more than 100 rockets a year. The plan adds two New Glenn launch pads at Cape Canaveral on top of two already under construction, plus a factory to produce up to 150 upper stages for a larger New Glenn variant.
insights.speaker: Eric Berger
insights.so_what: Blue Origin is building infrastructure for high-cadence heavy lift to compete directly with SpaceX for government and constellation demand.
insights.locator: Blue Origin goes bigger on New

insights.claim: Blue Origin plans to buy two more landing ships to recover New Glenn first stages, adding to its current ship Jacklyn, and to build a customer integration facility with four payload bays together with the US Space Force.
insights.speaker: Eric Berger
insights.so_what: Investment in recovery fleets and integration facilities shows Blue Origin expects many more launches and closer ties with the Space Force.
insights.quote: “These investments are centered on one goal: building the capacity to support more missions, more reliably, and more efficiently,”

themes.theme: Starship lunar refueling and catch attempts

insights.claim: NASA Aerospace Safety Advisory Panel member Charlie Precourt said the latest estimate for refueling flights needed to support a Starship lunar landing for Artemis is around 22, and that Artemis IV's many firsts reduce the likelihood of mission success.
insights.speaker: Eric Berger
insights.so_what: A refueling count that high raises the risk of Artemis schedule slips and puts pressure on Starship's flight cadence and the economics of its cryogenic transfer.
insights.quote: I think the last estimate is around 22 flights.

insights.claim: Elon Musk disputed the NASA safety panel's estimate of about 22 Starship refueling flights per lunar landing, saying the actual number will be more like 6 to 8.
insights.speaker: Eric Berger
insights.so_what: The roughly threefold gap between SpaceX and NASA estimates is a key uncertainty for the Artemis timeline.
insights.quote: “That’s way too high,” Musk said. “Actual number will be more like 6 to 8.”

insights.claim: SpaceX will try to catch both the Super Heavy booster and the Starship upper stage at Starbase on Starship's 15th test flight, targeted for November. Musk calls success "more likely than not", and Gwynne Shotwell expects the FAA license to include return to launch site over land, including northern Mexico, and tower catches for both stages.
insights.speaker: Eric Berger
insights.so_what: A successful catch of both stages would be a big step toward full reusability, which drives Starship's cost per launch.
insights.quote: “We have had significant constructive engagement with the FAA, and we expect the license for our Flight 15 to include return to launch site and tower catch for both stages,”

insights.claim: No new medium-lift rocket has debuted in the US in the 13 years since Orbital Sciences' Antares, which used Russian engines and a Ukrainian-built core stage. Four are now in development: Stoke Space's Nova, Relativity Space's Terran R, Rocket Lab's Neutron, and the Eclipse vehicle from Firefly and Northrop Grumman.
insights.speaker: Eric Berger
insights.so_what: Whichever of these vehicles debuts first could take national security and constellation demand that SpaceX is turning away.
insights.locator: Who will win the medium-lift launch

insights.claim: Rocket Lab is preparing the 98th Electron launch, carrying three HawkEye 360 satellites. Berger notes Rocket Lab remains only the second company to develop and frequently fly a purely commercial rocket.
insights.speaker: Eric Berger
insights.so_what: Electron's steady cadence supports Rocket Lab's credibility as it moves toward Neutron.
insights.locator: Rocket Lab sets next Electron launch

insights.claim: Spain's PLD Space has built three Miura 5 rockets, one of them for flight and two to qualify key systems. A fully integrated second stage is in qualification testing at its Teruel facility, and the company targets a first flight of the small-lift vehicle before mid-2027.
insights.speaker: Eric Berger
insights.so_what: Miura 5 could add sovereign European small-lift capacity; watch whether it flies before mid-2027.

insights.claim: Canadian launch startup Reaction Dynamics is seeking $350 million to grow from 68 to more than 350 staff. It aims to reach orbit with its small-lift Aurora rocket in 2028 and debut a medium-lift Borealis (6 tons to LEO, a little under half of Rocket Lab Neutron's advertised capacity) by 2031, dates Berger calls highly aspirational.
insights.speaker: Eric Berger
insights.so_what: Sovereign-access arguments are drawing capital to national launch startups, but the timelines are doubtful.
insights.quote: “We founded Reaction Dynamics because we believe Canada should be able to reach orbit on its own terms,”

insights.claim: Arianespace targets no earlier than November 23 for Ariane 6's return to flight after a liquid hydrogen turbopump anomaly. The flight is an Ariane 64 carrying 36 Amazon Leo satellites and will be the fifth Ariane 6 flight of 2026 and the tenth since July 2024.
insights.speaker: Eric Berger
insights.so_what: Ariane 6's cadence directly affects how fast Amazon's Leo constellation is deployed.

insights.claim: Japan launched the $578 million Martian Moons eXploration (MMX) mission on an H3 rocket in a new configuration with four solid boosters. The five-year mission will land on Phobos and return samples, something Russia's Phobos-Grunt attempted before it failed soon after launch in 2011.
insights.speaker: Eric Berger
insights.so_what: The upgraded H3 configuration extends Japan's sovereign capability for heavy interplanetary payloads.
insights.locator: Japanese rocket launches historic Phobos mission

insights.claim: A LandSpace Zhuque-2E rocket launched on September 15, released 10 satellites, then reignited and came down over the American Midwest. A farmer in rural Minnesota later found a circular metal object about 11 feet in diameter in a cornfield that experts link to the launch.
insights.speaker: Eric Berger
insights.so_what: Uncontrolled Chinese commercial-rocket debris over US territory could become a regulatory and diplomatic flashpoint.
insights.locator: Chinese rocket debris found in Midwest
